Hearing both sides, he finds his wife much at fault, the dispute arising from her fondness for Tom and displeasure with the rest of the household. Following high words with his wife, he resolves the wench shall go but will also take a course with the boy, whom he fears he has spoiled. To ease his mind, he settles accounts by making himself debtor for L117 5s. gained with joy the previous month, now relinquished for peace of mind, though troubled to be poorer than he thought; he stays up until nearly two in the morning with his accounts.

After being treated at Mr. Povy's, where Povy's excessive praise annoys him, Pepys takes the air with Creed and friends, then hosts music and supper at home, where he vexes Captain Taylor with an argument about Corant composition before laughing about it with Creed afterward. He and Creed sleep together in Mercer's bed.

canon.summary: Pepys spends the morning busy at the office and afternoon securing a warrant from Lord Treasurer, but is troubled to hear that Sir W. Batten and Sir J. Minnes notice his frequent absences from the office, which vexes him and which he hopes will make him mind his business better. He is more troubled by his omission to write to Mr. Coventry, and this night he falls asleep in the middle of the letter, committing forty blotts and blurrs. On the 30th, he works alone at his office making up monthly accounts with great accuracy, finding he has gained above L100 clear and is worth above L1400, the greatest sum ever. He dines with the modest Mr. Spong, enjoys discourse with him, then visits Woolwich and Deptford. He ends the month in great content about his estate but much trouble about expected difficulties with Tangier business, while great fears of the sickness spread in the City.

He chose not to vex himself about it further and they made peace. The day was spent on business, particularly investigating shipwrights who had deserted work for three days due to lack of money, and entertaining Lord Bruncker with a modest dinner. In the evening, a dispute arose over a finely written book of Rates being transcribed by Mr. Ackeworth's Dutch clerk for Captain Millet's mistress; Pepys and Lord Bruncker forced the woman to come, then cancelled the finished portions despite her concealed fury, which Pepys resented as spiteful. He walked with his wife until night, then sang briefly before bed, all the while in great trouble about his boy Tom who had been delayed at Greenwich overnight due to fear of the plague but finally returned home.

My Lord comes aboard from Greenwich and after discourse about trusting Cocke they part. They get a fisher boy by chance who, being odd and not answering aloud, nevertheless carries them safe thither with a mistake or two. In the way they are all surprised at the strange nature of the sea-water in a dark night, seeming like fire upon every stroke of the oar, which they say is a sign of wind. They go to the Crowne Inne at Rochester for supper, making merry with the poor fisher-boy who has not been in a bed in seven years since he came to 'prentice, and then in their clothes to bed.

canon.summary: The writer goes aboard the Prince and agrees a bargain of L5,000 with Sir Roger Cuttance for my Lord Sandwich for silk, cinnamon, nutmeggs, and indigo, nearly signing an undertaking for payment but escaping it by chance, for which he is later glad upon second thoughts. He visits Sir W. Pen where there is a pretty dinner and Sir W. Pen makes a bargain with Cocke for ten bales of silke. My Lord comes aboard from Greenwich and after discourse about trusting Cocke they part. Taking a wherry toward Chatham as it grows dark, they suffer great difficulties because their waterman does not know the way, going backward and forward in the dark night and wild place. They get a fisher boy by chance who, being odd and not answering aloud, nevertheless carries them safe thither with a mistake or two. In the way they are all surprised at the strange nature of the sea-water in a dark night, seeming like fire upon every stroke of the oar, which they say is a sign of wind. They go to the Crowne Inne at Rochester for supper, making merry with the poor fisher-boy who has not been in a bed in seven years since he came to 'prentice, and then in their clothes to bed.

After a merry dinner at Colonel Cleggat's, where he is followed by these poor wretches and gives them money, he takes ship to Woolwich to his wife. There he finds her in disorder due to a falling out with her maids, particularly Mary, who threatened to reveal something that would stop his wife's mouth, which he suspects concerns Brown. parsed.summary: This morning Pepys went to the office resolved to spend the whole day on business, agreeing with Poynter to be his clerk for the Victualling business. He spent all day alone in his little closet drawing up instructions for the Surveyours of the Ports, which Sir W. Coventry had long desired. After dinner he continued working, but at night a long discourse with Gibson, who was going to Yarmouth, made him understand how little he knew of the victualling business and the pursers' trade, leaving him ashamed and distrustful of all he had done that day. He set the work aside until the next morning, then went home by promise to his wife to have mirth there, with neighbours Miss Tooker and Mrs. Daniels coming to dance, and after supper he went to bed while they stayed merry below until two or three in the morning.

canon.summary: Pepys rises early on a fast-day and goes by water to the Duke of Albemarle, who has returned from Oxford and treats him with unusual kindness and deference, asking his advice on everything. The Duke surprises him with news that Lord Sandwich is to be Ambassador to Spain soon, which delights Pepys though he knows not the source. After a disappointing trip to church hoping to see Mrs. Pierce, Pepys spends the afternoon composing music, then goes with his wife and Mercer to Mrs. Pierce's, where an unexpected gathering of excellent musicians assembles, including the newly arrived Mr. Pierce from Oxford. Pepys passes the night in ecstasy at the music and the company of several attractive women, especially Mrs. Knipp who sings the noblest he ever heard, and learns from Pierce that the King has shown Lord Sandwich full public favor to remove any thoughts of discontent, confirming his embassy and reporting military promotions for the Dukes of York and Albemarle.

I sat talking till late, somewhat vexed by Madam Williams's snappish answer when I called her a mad jade, and more so by a letter from my Lord Duke of Albemarle pressing us to continue meetings all Christmas, which I had intended anyway but now see I must visit him often once my accounts are evened, though the frozen river hinders me. I then made up my Journal for eight or nine days, easing my mind, before supper and bed. The weather has been frosty eight or nine days, and we hope for abatement of the plague, else God have mercy upon us, for it will certainly continue next year if it does not.
